summary: This document describes a framework for supporting the Metro Ethernet Forum E-Tree service over an MPLS network. The goal is a simple approach to emulate E-Tree services in addition to E-LAN services on existing MPLS networks.

eli5.summary: In an E-Tree, branch offices can talk to the main office but not to each other, like a tree. This RFC explains how to build that using an existing MPLS network.

questions: what is the difference between e-lan and e-tree
what are root and leaf roles in e-tree
why can vpls not provide e-tree
subtitle: How an MPLS network can offer a root-and-leaf Ethernet service where branch sites reach the hub but not each other.

tldr.problem: The Metro Ethernet Forum defines an E-Tree service in which leaf sites may talk to root sites but never to each other, yet existing IETF Layer 2 VPN solutions give every attachment circuit any-to-any connectivity.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives a reference model in which every attachment circuit on a Virtual Service Instance is configured as Root or Leaf, with forwarding rules based on those roles, and it lists the gaps in VPLS and EVPN that must be filled.
tldr.outcome: It is a framework and gap analysis, not a protocol: it sets out what a solution must do and points to the requirements in RFC 7152.

facts.label: Frame types covered
facts.value: Known unicast, unknown unicast, broadcast, multicast

today: RFC 7387 is an Informational framework and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the architecture companion to the requirements in RFC 7152; it does not itself define a protocol.

sections.title: Introduction and Terminology
sections.content:
RFC 7387 describes a solution framework for the Metro Ethernet Forum (MEF) E-Tree service over a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) network. The aim is a simple and effective way to emulate E-Tree in addition to Ethernet LAN (E-LAN) services on an existing MPLS network. It extends the Layer 2 VPN framework of RFC 4664.

Each attachment circuit (AC), the link between a customer device and the provider edge (PE), has a role. A Root AC can send frames to any other AC in the service instance. A Leaf AC can send only to Root ACs, and a frame arriving on a Leaf AC must not be delivered to any Leaf AC.
sections.eli5: Some doors are marked Root and some are marked Leaf. Root doors can talk to every door. Leaf doors can only talk to Root doors.

sections.title: E-LAN, E-Tree and the Existing L2VPN Toolbox
sections.content:
MEF 6.1 defines two multipoint Ethernet service types: E-LAN, a multipoint-to-multipoint service, and E-Tree, a rooted-multipoint service. In an E-LAN every AC has the Root role, so any AC can reach any other. An E-Tree has one or more Root ACs and at least two Leaf ACs, supports communication among the roots and between a root and a leaf, and prohibits communication among the leaves.

The RFC reviews the IETF Layer 2 VPN solutions it builds on. VPLS (RFC 4761, RFC 4762) provides multipoint-to-multipoint Ethernet connectivity across IP/MPLS networks and may support E-LAN. EVPN uses an MP-BGP control plane to advertise MAC address reachability and supports active-active multihoming; at the time of writing it was still under development in the IETF. VPMS provides point-to-multipoint connectivity. The RFC states that existing IETF L2VPN solutions cannot support the E-Tree service.
sections.eli5: An E-LAN is a party where everyone can chat with everyone. An E-Tree is a party where the guests can only chat with the hosts, never with other guests.

sections.title: The E-Tree Reference Model
sections.content:
The reference model has three PEs, each holding a Virtual Service Instance (VSI) for the E-Tree service instance. Customer equipment attaches to the VSI over an AC, and each AC must be configured with a Root or Leaf role. A VSI keeps a MAC forwarding table isolated from other VSIs on the PE and also tracks the roles of its local ACs.

The forwarding rules hold whether the two ACs are on the same PE or on different PEs, and for all frame types: known unicast, unknown unicast, broadcast and multicast.

  • An egress frame at a Root AC must come from an ingress frame at a Root or Leaf AC of the same E-Tree instance.
  • An egress frame at a Leaf AC must come from an ingress frame at a Root AC of the same instance.

How frames cross the MPLS core depends on the solution. It could mesh VSIs with pseudowires as VPLS does, or follow the EVPN forwarding paradigm, in both cases constrained by the E-Tree rules. In most use cases there are only a few Root ACs but many Leaf ACs, and a PE may have only Root ACs or only Leaf ACs.
sections.eli5: Each provider box keeps a private address book for the service and remembers which of its doors are Root and which are Leaf. A message from a Leaf door is only ever handed to Root doors.

sections.title: E-Tree Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC lists eight major use cases. In each one a few central systems play the Root role and many edge systems play the Leaf role, for example a hub site and its spoke sites in a hub-and-spoke VPN, a mobile network controller and its base stations, or a video source and its subscribers.

Common to all the use cases, direct Layer 2 leaf-to-leaf communication is required to be prohibited. There may be one or several Root ACs, driven by a redundancy requirement or by having multiple serving sites. The RFC notes that for mobile backhaul the prohibition may not be valid for Long Term Evolution (LTE) X2 interfaces, which let two evolved Node Bs talk to each other.
sections.eli5: A TV station sends a show to many homes, and a company head office talks to its branches. In both cases the many ones on the edge only talk to the one in the middle.

sections.title: Gaps in L2VPN for E-Tree
sections.content:
The RFC names two major gaps. First, IP/MPLS L2VPN has no differentiation of AC roles: it supports any-to-any connectivity and has no way to constrain forwarding by role, while MEF E-Tree defines forwarding rules based on the originating and receiving roles.

Second, there is no AC role indication or advertisement. When a PE receives a frame from another PE over the MPLS core, it cannot tell whether the frame came from a Root AC or a Leaf AC, which matters most when that PE has both kinds of AC on the VSI.

Other desirable properties are a Leaf-only PE, which other PEs need not send leaf-originated frames to, and compatibility with existing PEs whose single-role ACs count as roots. These are described in the requirements document, RFC 7152.
sections.eli5: Today the network has no way to put a Root or Leaf sticker on a message, so the box at the far end cannot tell which kind of door it came from.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An E-Tree may be deployed for security reasons, to prohibit communication among leaf sites. A solution must therefore enforce the E-Tree forwarding constraints and must guarantee that Ethernet frames do not leak outside the E-Tree service instance they belong to.

The RFC warns that E-Tree does not know about higher-layer security constraints, so applications generally cannot rely on it for protection unless all their security constraints are fully implemented by the service. A solution built on VPLS or EVPN inherits the control-plane and data-plane issues described in the L2VPN framework, RFC 4664.
sections.eli5: Keeping branch shops from talking to each other is a useful rule, but it is not a full lock. Anything that needs real secrecy still needs its own protection.
